cse-2026-1-ga-1.approach: A *protagonist* is the leading character who drives the story; its opposite is the character who opposes them. Recognise the roots *pro-* (for) and *anti-* (against) on the same stem *-agonist* (contender).

steps.title: Meaning of the given word
steps.body: *Protagonist* (Greek *prōtos* 'first' + *agōnistēs* 'contender'): the main character or the leading supporter of a cause.

steps.title: Find its opposite among the options
steps.body: *Antagonist* (*ant-* 'against' + *agōnistēs*) is the opponent or adversary of the protagonist, the one who acts **against** them. It is the direct opposite.

steps.title: Eliminate the look-alikes
steps.body: The other words only sound similar: an *agnostic* is unsure whether God exists, an *arsonist* sets fires on purpose, an *anarchist* rejects all government. None is opposite in meaning to *protagonist*.

optionAnalysis.reason: *Agnostic*: a person who holds that God's existence cannot be known. It sounds like the other words but has nothing to do with protagonist.
*Antagonist*: the opponent of the protagonist, the exact opposite role.
*Arsonist*: someone who deliberately sets fire to property. Unrelated in meaning.
*Anarchist*: someone who rejects all government. Unrelated in meaning.

cse-2026-1-ga-1.shortcut: Same stem *-agonist*, opposite prefix: pro-tagonist vs. ant-agonist.
pitfalls: Picking a word just because it starts with 'a-' and sounds similar (agnostic, anarchist).
cse-2026-1-ga-1.verification: In any story the hero and the villain are the protagonist and the antagonist, a standard antonym pair.

cse-2026-1-ga-2.approach: Every piece covers exactly 4 tiles, so a shape built from them must have a tile count divisible by 4. Count the tiles in each option, then check that the shapes passing the count can really be tiled.
cse-2026-1-ga-2.given:
Pieces: a $2 \times 2$ square and a $1 \times 4$ bar (each 4 tiles, any orientation, no overlaps).

| Option | Shape | Tiles |
|---|---|---|
| A | $2 \times 4$ | 8 |
| B | $3 \times 4$ | 12 |
| C | $3 \times 5$ | 15 |
| D | $4 \times 5$ | 20 |

steps.title: Necessary condition: tile count is a multiple of 4
steps.body:
If $a$ squares and $b$ bars are used, the shape has $4a + 4b = 4(a+b)$ tiles, always a multiple of 4.

$8 = 4 \times 2$, $12 = 4 \times 3$, $20 = 4 \times 5$, but $15 = 4 \times 3 + 3$. So **C ($3 \times 5$) is impossible**.

steps.title: The other three can actually be built
steps.body:
- **A** ($2 \times 4$): two $2 \times 2$ squares side by side (or two horizontal bars).
- **B** ($3 \times 4$): three horizontal $1 \times 4$ bars, one per row.
- **D** ($4 \times 5$): five vertical $1 \times 4$ bars, one per column.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: A, B and D have explicit tilings; C fails the area test ($15 \bmod 4 = 3$). So the only shape that **cannot** be constructed is **C**, the $3 \times 5$ block.

optionAnalysis.reason: $2 \times 4$ = 8 tiles: two $2 \times 2$ squares side by side.
$3 \times 4$ = 12 tiles: three $1 \times 4$ bars laid horizontally, one per row.
$3 \times 5$ = 15 tiles, not a multiple of 4, so no combination of 4-tile pieces can cover it exactly.
$4 \times 5$ = 20 tiles: five $1 \times 4$ bars standing vertically, one per column.

cse-2026-1-ga-2.shortcut: Only the area matters here: the one option whose tile count is not divisible by 4 ($15$) is the answer.
pitfalls: Trying to fit $2 \times 2$ squares into an odd-width block and concluding D or B is impossible, without remembering the bar can be rotated.
Assuming divisibility by 4 is enough in general; here it is, but you should still exhibit a tiling for each remaining option.
cse-2026-1-ga-2.verification: Explicit tilings were given for A, B and D, and the area argument rules out C, so exactly one option fails.

cse-2026-1-ga-3.approach: Count eliminations, not rounds: every game produces exactly one loser who leaves, and all players except the winner must leave. So games = players − 1.

steps.title: One game, one elimination
steps.body: There are no ties and the loser of each game is eliminated, so each game removes **exactly one** player. Conversely every eliminated player lost exactly one game (her last).

steps.title: Count the players to eliminate
steps.body: The tournament ends when one undefeated player is left, so $64 - 1 = 63$ players are eliminated, which takes **63 games**.

steps.title: Cross-check round by round
steps.body: With 64 players the rounds pair up cleanly: $32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 63$ games.

optionAnalysis.reason: $127 = 2 \times 64 - 1$ is the number of games in a *double*-elimination style count, or the number of nodes in the full bracket tree (players + games); not the number of games.
$64$ would need one elimination more than there are losers: one player must stay undefeated.
$63 = 64 - 1$: one game per eliminated player.
$32$ counts only the first round.

cse-2026-1-ga-3.shortcut: In any single-elimination tournament with $n$ players, games $= n - 1$ (the bracket shape does not matter).
pitfalls: Adding the number of players and games, or doubling, to get 127.
Stopping after the first round (32).

cse-2026-1-ga-4.approach: Electives get whatever is left after the fixed and minimum requirements, so maximise the total (70) and give specialization only its minimum (10).
concepts: Maximise by pushing others to bounds
cse-2026-1-ga-4.given:
| Component | Constraint |
|---|---|
| Total | $60 \le T \le 70$ |
| Core | exactly 15 |
| Project | exactly 20 |
| Specialization | $\ge 10$ |
| Elective | maximise |

steps.title: Write electives in terms of the rest
steps.body: $E = T - 15 - 20 - S_p = T - 35 - S_p$, where $T$ is the total and $S_p$ the specialization credits.

steps.title: Push the other variables to their bounds
steps.body:
$E$ grows with $T$ and shrinks with $S_p$, so take $T = 70$ (the maximum) and $S_p = 10$ (the minimum):
$$E_{\max} = 70 - 15 - 20 - 10 = 25$$

steps.title: Check feasibility
steps.body: $15 + 20 + 10 + 25 = 70$, which lies in $[60, 70]$, and every individual requirement holds. So 25 elective credits are achievable.

optionAnalysis.reason: $10$ is feasible (it leaves $70 - 15 - 20 - 10 = 25$ for specialization) but not the largest; it repeats the specialization minimum, a likely mix-up.
$15 = 60 - 15 - 20 - 10$ uses the **minimum** total 60 instead of the maximum 70.
$20$ would leave $70 - 15 - 20 - 20 = 15$ for specialization, which is allowed but does not maximise electives.
$25 = 70 - 15 - 20 - 10$: maximum total, minimum specialization.

cse-2026-1-ga-4.shortcut: Max elective = max total − fixed parts − minimum of the other variable part $= 70 - 35 - 10 = 25$.
pitfalls: Using the minimum total 60 (gives 15).
Forgetting the 10-credit specialization minimum (gives 35, not an option).
cse-2026-1-ga-4.verification: Any $E > 25$ would force $T = 35 + S_p + E > 35 + 10 + 25 = 70$, breaking the upper limit.

cse-2026-1-ga-5.approach: Write the statement as an implication $T \Rightarrow (\text{all stand} \wedge \text{all silent})$. Its contrapositive and any weakening of its conclusion must be true; its converse need not be.
cse-2026-1-ga-5.given:
$T$: the teacher is in the room. $St$: all students stand. $Si$: all students are silent.

Given: $T \Rightarrow (St \wedge Si)$.

steps.title: Weakening the conclusion keeps truth
steps.body: From $T \Rightarrow (St \wedge Si)$ we get both $T \Rightarrow Si$ (option B) and $T \Rightarrow St$ (option D), because $St \wedge Si$ implies each part.

steps.title: The contrapositive is equivalent
steps.body: $T \Rightarrow (St \wedge Si)$ is equivalent to $\neg(St \wedge Si) \Rightarrow \neg T$: if not all students are standing silently, i.e. **some student is not standing silently**, the teacher is not in the room. That is option A, so A is necessarily true.

steps.title: The converse does not follow
steps.body: Option C says $St \Rightarrow T$, the converse (of a weakened form). Students could all be standing for some other reason (say, the national anthem) with no teacher present; the given statement is not violated. So C is **not necessarily true**.

answer.value: "If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room." — option (C)

optionAnalysis.reason: Contrapositive of the given statement: $\neg(St \wedge Si) \Rightarrow \neg T$. Always true when the statement is true.
$T \Rightarrow Si$ follows by dropping the 'standing' part of the conclusion.
$St \Rightarrow T$ is a converse; the statement says nothing about what happens when the teacher is absent, so this need not hold.
$T \Rightarrow St$ follows by dropping the 'silent' part of the conclusion.

cse-2026-1-ga-5.shortcut: In 'not necessarily true' questions on an if-then statement, look for the converse (or inverse) — here the option that reverses the arrow.
pitfalls: Treating 'when the teacher is in the room' as 'if and only if'.
Misreading the contrapositive (A) as an inverse; it negates *and* swaps, so it is equivalent.
cse-2026-1-ga-5.verification: Counter-example world for C: no teacher, all students standing and chatting. The given statement holds (vacuously, since $T$ is false) but C is false. No such world exists for A, B or D.

cse-2026-1-ga-6.approach: Check each statement against the exact quantifier the passage uses: it says combinatorial counting is **sometimes** used in modeling, and describes probabilities being assigned to compute averages.

steps.title: Statement P
steps.body: P claims combinatorics is **always** invoked in modeling physical phenomena. The passage says this kind of counting is "**sometimes** used in the modeling of several physical phenomena". 'Sometimes' contradicts 'always', so **P is false**.

steps.title: Statement Q
steps.body: The passage says that in such models "the different combinatorial possibilities are assigned probability values" and that this "enables the computation of the average values of physical quantities". Q says exactly that modeling *some* phenomena involves this: **Q is true**.

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: P false, Q true is option **(B)**. Note the passage never needs to say Q word for word; Q is a faithful restatement with the safe quantifier *some*.

answer.value: P is False and Q is True — option (B)

optionAnalysis.reason: Q is directly supported by the last two sentences of the passage, so it cannot be false.
P overstates 'sometimes' as 'always'; Q paraphrases the passage.
Gets both wrong: P is contradicted and Q is supported.
P is contradicted by the word 'sometimes'.

cse-2026-1-ga-6.shortcut: Spot the absolute word: 'always' in P against 'sometimes' in the passage kills P; Q uses the safe 'some'.
pitfalls: Accepting P because combinatorics is important in physics in general — only what the passage supports counts.
cse-2026-1-ga-6.verification: Q uses the weak quantifier 'some', matching 'often, in such models'; P uses a universal one that the passage explicitly limits.

cse-2026-1-ga-7.approach: Turn the two views into a height map (number of cubes in each column of the $3 \times 3$ footprint): the front view gives each column's maximum height and, through its face edges, which depth row each face comes from; the top view gives the footprint and which cells share a height. Then compare with the four structures.
cse-2026-1-ga-7.given: Rows are listed **back / middle / front**, columns **left → right**; each entry is the number of stacked cubes.

steps.title: Read the top view
steps.body: The footprint is $3 \times 3$ **minus the front-right cell**. Faces: the left column's back two cells share one height; its front cell has another; the back row of the right two columns is one face; the middle row of the right two columns plus the front-middle cell form one L-shaped face (same height).

The bottom-right square is a separate face (it comes from the middle row, since the front-right cell is empty). The rectangle across middle + right at height 1–2 is one face, so it comes from the **back row** (heights 2, 2). The top-left square is set back, so the left column's back cells are 3 tall.

| back | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| middle | 3 | 1 | 1 |
| front | 2 | 1 | 0 |

The top view's L-face (middle row right two cells + front middle cell) indeed all have height 1.

- (ii): middle row $3, 2, 1$ — the middle cube is 2 tall, so the top view would merge it with the back row and the front view would show a step at depth 1. ✗

(ii) has a 2-tall cube in the centre of the middle row; the top view would then show the middle-row centre at the same level as the back row, not joined with the front-middle cell.

pitfalls: Comparing only outlines: the outline of (ii)'s top view is the same as (iv)'s — the internal face edges are what separate them.
Mixing up which way the 'front' arrow points in the 3D drawings.

cse-2026-1-ga-8.approach: Each $H_K(S)$ is a 'hinge': 0 up to $S = K$, then slope 1. The graph has a slope change $+1$ at $S = 10$ and $-1$ at $S = 20$, so $N(S) = H_{10}(S) - H_{20}(S)$. Then confirm by evaluating at a few points.
cse-2026-1-ga-8.given: From the graph: $N(S) = 0$ for $S \le 10$; rises linearly to $N(20) = 10$ (slope $\frac{10}{10} = 1$); $N(S) = 10$ for $S \ge 20$.

steps.title: Shape of one hinge
steps.body: $H_K(S) = \max(S - K, 0)$ is $0$ for $S \le K$ and $S - K$ (slope $+1$) for $S > K$. Adding $c\,H_K$ to a function changes its slope by $c$ at $S = K$ and nowhere else.

steps.title: Read off the slope changes
steps.body:
The graph's slope is $0$ before 10, $1$ between 10 and 20, and $0$ after 20. So the slope jumps by $+1$ at $S = 10$ and by $-1$ at $S = 20$, giving
$$N(S) = H_{10}(S) - H_{20}(S)$$

optionAnalysis.reason: $H_{10} - H_{20}$: 0 until 10, slope 1 until 20, then flat at 10 — exactly the graph.
$H_{10} - 2H_{20}$ has slope $1 - 2 = -1$ after 20, so it falls back to 0 at $S = 30$ instead of staying at 10.
$-H_{10} + H_{20}$ is the mirror image: it goes **down** to $-10$ between 10 and 20.
$H_{15} - H_{20}$ starts rising only at 15 and levels off at $20 - 15 = 5$, not 10.

cse-2026-1-ga-8.shortcut: Evaluate at $S = 15$ (graph gives 5): A gives 5, B gives 5, C gives $-5$, D gives 0. Then at $S = 30$ (graph gives 10): A gives 10, B gives 0. Only A survives.
pitfalls: Thinking the plateau needs $-2H_{20}$ to 'cancel' the rise — subtracting one hinge already makes the slope 0.
cse-2026-1-ga-8.verification: Table check at $S = 5, 15, 20, 30$ matches the graph at every point, and both sides are piecewise linear with the same breakpoints.

cse-2026-1-ga-9.approach: Use the medal order (Chopra > Vadlejch > Vesely) together with 'after four rounds Vesely was second' to place Vesely's best throw, then eliminate rounds one at a time.

steps.title: Rule out rounds 1, 2, 5 and 6
steps.body:
- Rounds 1–2: by (i), Vadlejch and Vesely had no medal-winning throws there, and Vesely's best throw is his bronze-medal throw.
- Rounds 5–6: by (iii), Vesely could not improve on his best after round 4 (and his round-6 throw was a foul by (ii)).

So his best throw came in round 3 or 4.

steps.title: Rule out round 4
steps.body: By (iv), Vadlejch's round-4 throw was the best in that round, so it beat Vesely's round-4 throw. By (iii), after four rounds Vesely was **second**, i.e. ahead of Vadlejch — so Vesely's best so far beat Vadlejch's round-4 throw. Hence Vesely's best is not his round-4 throw.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: Only round 3 remains: Vesely threw his best (bronze-medal) throw in the **third** round. (Vadlejch later overtook him in round 5, since his round-6 throw was a foul.)

optionAnalysis.reason: Round 3 is the only round left after clues (i)–(iv) are applied.
In round 4 Vadlejch beat Vesely, yet Vesely was ahead of Vadlejch after round 4, so his best came earlier.
Clue (iii): Vesely could not improve after round 4.
Clue (ii): Vesely's sixth throw was a foul (and (iii) also excludes it).

cse-2026-1-ga-9.shortcut: Rounds 1–2 and 5–6 are excluded outright; the round-4 clue about Vadlejch is there only to exclude round 4.
pitfalls: Choosing round 4 because Vesely was second 'after four rounds' — that position came from an earlier throw.
cse-2026-1-ga-9.verification: A consistent scenario: Vesely's best in round 3, Vadlejch's round-4 throw shorter than it, Vadlejch's silver throw in round 5. All four clues hold.

cse-2026-1-ga-10.approach: There are 36 equally likely ordered outcomes. For each first roll $a$, count the multiples of $a$ in $\{1, \dots, 6\}$, which is $\lfloor 6/a \rfloor$.

steps.title: Sample space
steps.body: Two rolls of a fair die: $6 \times 6 = 36$ equally likely ordered pairs (first, second).

steps.title: Count favourable pairs by the first roll

optionAnalysis.reason: $\frac16 = \frac{6}{36}$ counts only the doubles (second roll equal to the first), i.e. the multiple $1 \times a$.
$\frac{5}{18} = \frac{10}{36}$ undercounts by 4 pairs, e.g. missing the doubles 3–3, 4–4, 5–5, 6–6.
$\frac{14}{36} = \frac{7}{18}$, the correct count.
$\frac56$ is far too large; it is close to $1 - \frac16$, the chance the two rolls differ.

pitfalls: Forgetting that a number is a multiple of itself ($1 \times a$), which drops the 6 doubles.
Counting unordered pairs instead of the 36 ordered outcomes.

cse-2026-1-cs-1.approach: After two steps there are 4 balls; equal counts means 2 red + 2 blue, i.e. one red draw and one blue draw. Sum the two paths of the probability tree.

steps.title: What 'equal' means after two steps
steps.body: Each step adds one ball, so after two steps the urn holds $2 + 2 = 4$ balls. Equal numbers means **2 red, 2 blue**, which happens exactly when one draw was red and the other blue (RB or BR).

steps.title: Path R then B
steps.body: $P(R_1) = \frac12$; the urn becomes 2R 1B, so $P(B_2 \mid R_1) = \frac13$. Path probability $= \frac12 \times \frac13 = \frac16$.

steps.title: Path B then R, and add
steps.body:
By symmetry $P(B_1)P(R_2 \mid B_1) = \frac12 \times \frac13 = \frac16$.
$$P(\text{2R 2B}) = \frac16 + \frac16 = \frac13$$

optionAnalysis.reason: $\frac14$ treats the draws as independent fair coin flips ($\frac12 \cdot \frac12$) and counts only one order.
$\frac13$: two paths, each $\frac12 \cdot \frac13$.
$\frac12 = 2 \cdot \frac12 \cdot \frac12$ ignores that the urn's composition changes after the first draw (the second draw is not 50-50).
$\frac23$ is the probability of the **unequal** outcomes (3R1B or 1R3B).

cse-2026-1-cs-1.shortcut: Pólya urn fact: starting from 1 red and 1 blue, after $n$ steps the number of added red balls is uniform on $\{0, 1, \dots, n\}$. For $n = 2$: P(exactly 1 red added) $= \frac13$.
pitfalls: Using $\frac12$ for the second draw — the drawn ball is returned **with an extra copy**, so the urn is 2:1.
Counting only one of the two orders (gives $\frac16$).
cse-2026-1-cs-1.verification: Leaf probabilities: 3R1B $= \frac12 \cdot \frac23 = \frac13$, 2R2B $= \frac13$, 1R3B $= \frac13$; they sum to 1 and are uniform as the Pólya-urn shortcut predicts.

cse-2026-1-cs-2.approach: Fill the top-left $3 \times 3$ block freely; the last column and last row are then forced by the parity rule, and the corner entry is forced consistently. So the count is $2^{9}$.

steps.title: The $3 \times 3$ block is free
steps.body:
Choose entries $a_{ij}$ for $1 \le i, j \le 3$ arbitrarily: $2^9 = 512$ ways. Example (highlighted):
$$\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}$$

steps.title: Last column and last row are forced
steps.body:
For rows $1$–$3$, $a_{i4}$ must make the row sum even: $a_{i4} = (a_{i1} + a_{i2} + a_{i3}) \bmod 2$. Here rows sum to $1, 2, 2$, so $a_{14}, a_{24}, a_{34} = 1, 0, 0$.

For columns $1$–$3$, $a_{4j} = (a_{1j} + a_{2j} + a_{3j}) \bmod 2$: columns sum to $2, 2, 1$, so $a_{41}, a_{42}, a_{43} = 0, 0, 1$.

steps.title: The corner is forced consistently
steps.body:
Row 4 needs $a_{44} \equiv a_{41} + a_{42} + a_{43}$; column 4 needs $a_{44} \equiv a_{14} + a_{24} + a_{34}$. Both right-hand sides equal $\sum_{i,j \le 3} a_{ij} \pmod 2$, so they always agree. Here both give $1$.

Every free choice extends to **exactly one** valid matrix, and every valid matrix arises this way, so the count is $2^9 = 512$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $2^{(4-1)(4-1)} = 2^9 = 512$: one matrix per choice of the free $3 \times 3$ block.
$1025 = 2^{10} + 1$ has no counting meaning here (it double-counts the corner and adds one).
$1023 = 2^{10} - 1$ looks like 'all non-empty subsets' of 10 items; the parity system leaves 9 free bits, not 10.
$255 = 2^8 - 1$ undercounts and wrongly excludes the zero matrix (which has 0 ones everywhere, an even number).

cse-2026-1-cs-2.shortcut: For $m \times n$ binary matrices with all row and column sums even, the count is $2^{(m-1)(n-1)}$. For $4 \times 4$: $2^9$.
pitfalls: Forgetting the all-zero matrix counts (zero is even).
Treating the 8 parity equations as independent: only 7 are, since the sum of all row equations equals the sum of all column equations — giving $2^{16-7} = 2^9$.
cse-2026-1-cs-2.verification: Linear algebra over GF(2): 16 unknowns, 8 parity equations of rank 7, so the solution space has dimension $16 - 7 = 9$ and $2^9 = 512$ elements.

cse-2026-1-cs-3.approach: Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial $\det(A - \lambda I)$, which has degree $n$; a root's multiplicity is at most the degree, and the identity matrix attains $n$.

steps.title: Upper bound
steps.body: For an $n \times n$ real matrix $A$, $p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$ is a polynomial of degree exactly $n$. The (algebraic) multiplicity of an eigenvalue $\lambda_0$ is the power of $(\lambda - \lambda_0)$ dividing $p$, so it is at most $n$. The geometric multiplicity is at most the algebraic one, so also $\le n$.

steps.title: The bound is attained
steps.body: $A = I_n$ has $p(\lambda) = (1 - \lambda)^n$, so $\lambda = 1$ has multiplicity $n$ (algebraic and geometric: every vector is an eigenvector). Likewise $cI_n$ for any real $c$, and the zero matrix.

steps.title: Compare with the options
steps.body: Maximum $= n$ (upper bound met by $I_n$). $n + 1$ exceeds the degree of $p(\lambda)$; $n - 1$ and $1$ are values some matrices have, but $I_n$ shows they are not the maximum.

optionAnalysis.reason: Multiplicity $\le \deg p = n$, and $I_n$ attains $n$.
$n - 1$ is not the maximum: $I_n$ has an eigenvalue of multiplicity $n$.
$1$ is the multiplicity when all eigenvalues are distinct, not the maximum possible.
$n + 1$ exceeds the degree $n$ of the characteristic polynomial, impossible.

cse-2026-1-cs-3.shortcut: Think of the identity matrix: one eigenvalue repeated $n$ times, and no polynomial of degree $n$ has a root of multiplicity above $n$.
pitfalls: Confusing 'maximum multiplicity' with the number of distinct eigenvalues.
Thinking repeated eigenvalues need complex entries — real scalar matrices already repeat one eigenvalue $n$ times.
cse-2026-1-cs-3.verification: Sum of algebraic multiplicities over all (complex) eigenvalues is exactly $n$, so a single eigenvalue can take all $n$, never more.
